state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of alternate angles like a seesaw at the playground. Just because one side goes up doesn't mean the other side has to go up the same amount. In the same way, alternate angles can be different sizes, not always equal. So, in this case, Tom is correct that angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate, but they may not be equal.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I get that alternate angles can be different sizes, like the seesaw example. But if they’re on opposite sides of the transversal, why do some people say they’re equal? Can you explain that a bit more?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of alternate angles like a pair of shoes - just because they're on opposite sides of your feet doesn't mean they're always the same size. Sometimes they match, but not always. So, even though angles \( p \) and \( q \) are on opposite sides of the transversal, they can still be different sizes.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies to tell the student that alternate angles aren't always equal but never addresses the critical condition (parallel lines) that determines when they are equal, and the student's final turn shows they remain confused about when alternate angles are equal versus when they aren't.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses concrete analogies (seesaw, shoes), these analogies are misleading and mathematically incorrect, as they fail to convey that alternate angles ARE equal when lines are parallel, undermining the educational value of the experiential approach.
